questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Dimension of a Polynomial Vector Space Given Its Standard Monomial Basis
questions.problem: What is the dimension of ${R}_{15}[t]$, the vector space of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $15?$
questions.worked_solution:
The standard basis of ${R}_{n}[t]$ is

$$
{1,\,t,\,{t}^{2},\,…,\,{t}^{n}}.
$$

So, the standard basis of ${R}_{15}[t]$ is 

$$
{1,\,t,\,{t}^{2},\,…,\,{t}^{15}}.
$$

Therefore, we have that 

$$
\text{dim}({R}_{15}[t])=15+1=16.
$$

In general,

$$
\text{dim}({R}_{n}[t])=n+1.
$$

questions.problem: What is the dimension of ${\text{M}}_{5}(R),$ the vector space of all $5\times 5$ matrices over $R?$
questions.worked_solution:
The standard basis of ${\text{M}}_{n}(R)$ contains a total of ${n}^{2}$ matrices, each with one nonzero entry that is equal to $1.$ 

For example, the standard basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ contains ${2}^{2}=4$ elements, and is given by

$$
{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}.
$$

Therefore, for ${\text{M}}_{5}(R),$ we have

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{5}(R))={5}^{2}=25.
$$

In general, 

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{n}(R))={n}^{2}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Finite and Infinite-Dimensional Vector Spaces
questions.problem:
Which of the following vector spaces are finite-dimensional?

- ${ℓ}^{1},$ the vector space of infinite real sequences where the sum of the absolute values of the terms are finite
- ${R}_{3000}[t],$ the vector space of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $3\,000$
- ${\text{M}}_{50\times 60}(R),$ the vector space of all $50\times 60$ matrices over $R$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine our vector spaces.

- ${ℓ}^{1}$ is *not* finite-dimensional. To understand why, we first note that the following subset of ${ℓ}^{1}$ is linearly independent: 

$$
{{e}_{1},\,{e}_{2},\,…,{e}_{n}},\,n\in N
$$

where, for each $j\in {1,2,…,n},$

$$
{e}_{j}=(0,…,0,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{1,}_{{↑}_{{j}^{\text{th}}\text{ position}}}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,0,…).
$$

Indeed, we have that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=0}^{n}{x}_{i}{e}_{i}=0
$$

if and only if ${x}_{i}=0$ for all $i=0,1,2,…,n.$ Therefore,  for any  $n\in N,$  there exists a linearly independent subset of ${ℓ}^{1}$ of size $n,$ which imples that  ${ℓ}^{1}$ cannot have finite dimension.

- ${R}_{3000}[t]$ and  ${\text{M}}_{50\times 60}(R)$ are finite-dimensional. Indeed,

$$
\text{dim}({R}_{3000}[t])=3\,000+1=3\,001,
$$

and

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{50\times 60}(R))=50\cdot 60=3\,000
$$

 
are both finite numbers.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following vector spaces are finite-dimensional?

- ${\text{M}}_{250\times 100}(R),$ the vector space of all $250\times 100$ matrices over $R$
- $R[t],$ the vector space of all polynomial functions in the variable $t$
- ${R}_{10}[t],$ the vector space of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $10$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine our vector spaces.

- $R[t]$ is *not* finite-dimensional. To understand why, we first note that the following set of (polynomial) functions is linearly independent:

$$
{1,\,t,\,{t}^{2},\,…,{t}^{n}},\,n\in N.
$$

Indeed, we have that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=0}^{n}{a}_{i}{t}^{i}=0
$$

for all $t\in R$ if and only if ${a}_{i}=0$ for all $i=0,1,2,…,n.$ Therefore,  for any  $n\in N,$  there exists a linearly independent subset of $R[t]$ of size $n,$ which imples that $R[t]$ cannot have finite dimension.

- ${\text{M}}_{250\times 100}(R)$ and ${R}_{10}[t]$ are finite-dimensional. Indeed, 

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{250\times 100}(R))=250\cdot 100=25\,000
$$

 
and

$$
\text{dim}({R}_{10}[t])=10+1=11,
$$

are both finite numbers.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."
